title: The four hinges (CCC 1805–1809)
hook: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, on which a good life turns

segments.voice: Yesterday, the theological virtues: faith, hope and charity, given by God. Your line was the greatest is charity. Did you drop the anchor once? Today, four more virtues, the ones people build by practice. Day three hundred fourteen.

Look at the nearest door. It's heavy. Maybe solid wood, maybe steel. But everything it does, opening, closing, letting people in, keeping the cold out, depends on a few small pieces of metal on one side that you never look at. The hinges. Take them off and the best door in the world is just a slab leaning against a wall. The ancient world had a word for hinge, and the Church borrowed it to name four virtues. You already know the word from somewhere else: men in red hats, and a red bird. Today, the four hinges.
screen: `A HEAVY DOOR.` → `SMALL PIECES OF METAL.` → `WITHOUT THEM, A SLAB.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Cardinal comes from the Latin cardo: hinge. The cardinal virtues are the four on which a good life turns. The cardinals of the Church share the root, as hinges of the Church in Rome, and the red bird was named after the red of their robes. Second, where the four come from. Greek philosophers like Plato named them long before Christ. And the Bible names them too, in the book of Wisdom, in the Douay-Rheims: "she teacheth temperance, and prudence, and justice, and fortitude." Christian writers like Ambrose and Augustine took them up, and the Church still teaches them. Third, the four, one at a time. Prudence is practical wisdom: seeing what's actually good here, now, and the right way to do it. The Catechism calls it the charioteer of the virtues, because it steers the others. Justice is the steady will to give God and neighbor what is their due. Fortitude is courage and firmness: holding on to the good when it's hard, resisting fear, even the fear of death. Temperance is balance: enjoying good things without being ruled by them. Fourth, how they grow. Unlike faith, hope and charity, which Catholics say are given, these four are human virtues: they're built by practice, choice by choice, like muscles, and God's grace helps them grow. A person who keeps telling the truth when it's awkward becomes just. A person who keeps saying enough becomes temperate. And the door swings easier every time.
screen: `CARDO: HINGE.` · `PLATO, WISDOM, AMBROSE.` · `PRUDENCE STEERS THE OTHERS.` · `BUILT BY PRACTICE, LIKE MUSCLE.` · then, large: `TEMPERANCE, PRUDENCE, JUSTICE, FORTITUDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice one of the four. Settle, and breathe. Say them slowly: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance. Which door in your life is sticking? Maybe you need prudence for a decision. Justice for someone you owe something to, even just credit. Fortitude for a hard conversation. Temperance for the thing you always have too much of. Choose one. Picture using it once today, in one specific moment. If you pray, you can ask for help with it. The bell holds the time.
Cardinal virtues. From the Latin for hinge: prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance, the four human virtues on which a good life turns. Today's word.
Your line: the hinges. Today, every time you walk through a door, name the one virtue you chose, and look for your moment to use it. Day three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching, from catechism classes to confession, uses the four cardinal virtues as a map of the good life, and many Catholics choose one to work on during a season like Lent.
